thread.title: Apple (AAPL): Facts Beat Fear And Feelings

author: Martin Tillier
title: Apple (AAPL): Facts Beat Fear And Feelings
text:
Apple earnings (Shutterstock photo)
Traders and investors who follow Apple ( AAPL ), which, let’s be honest, is almost all of us, should be going into Thursday's Q4 earnings release with a sense of what Yogi Berra famously referred to as “Déjà vu all over again”. As is so often the case, there are a bunch of stories out there stating that the report will be a major disappointment.
This time around, most are focused on what they consider to be potentially weak demand for the iPhone X, and as a result the stock has lost nearly eight percent over the last couple of weeks, even as the broader market has continued to hit new highs.
So, should we be worried, or pleased to be offered a discount on the stock?
Regular readers will not be surprised to hear that I believe it to be the latter. I have been a consistent bull on AAPL since it was trading at around half its current price a couple of years ago, mostly because, despite all the angst, the consumer electronics giant continues to grow. Yes, there was a wobble for a while a few years back as the transition from the company’s legendary CEO Steve Jobs to Tim Cook seemed to stall progress for a while, but with hindsight that only set up the company for more robust growth over the last couple of years.
There is, apparently, something in some people’s psyche that makes them root against success, so it is no surprise that there is a legion of doubters out there who lap up every downgrade and negative story, but this round of negativity, even more than most, flies in the face of what actual evidence we have.
Apple does not give out much information on specific products, but based on reports from retailers, some analysts have concluded that the iPhone X was the best selling device in Q4. That sounds better than it is, as what counts for the stock is how that performance stacks up against expectations already priced in, and most of the numbers being bandied about miss on that basis. There are, however, two problems here.
The first is the obvious fact that these are not reported numbers, but estimates, or, in common parlance, guesses. When analysts guess, they tend to miss low, as proven by the fact that somewhere between 65 and 70 percent of S&P 500 companies beat consensus estimates every quarter during earnings season. (If you are curious, so far this time around, 77 percent of companies have beaten the consensus estimate.)
That makes sense when you consider who they are guessing for. Investors who maybe miss an opportunity because of an overly pessimistic analysis usually just shrug their shoulders; those that lose money because the analyst missed on the optimistic side tend to complain, and even move their accounts.
The second is that, when looked at from another angle, there is contradictory evidence that suggests that things are nowhere near as bad as the guesses would suggest. Because Apple doesn’t give out much information beyond what is required, those that watch the stock often look to the company’s suppliers for a sense of how product sales are going and expected to grow. This quarter that evidence suggests that far from being a huge disappointment, iPhone X sales are at least on target.
Suppliers such as the Japanese company Murata Manufacturing have said that they have seen no reduction in orders that would indicate weak sales, and on Monday the indications from the Austrian supplier of optical sensors for the new phone, AMS AG, suggested just the opposite. They reported stronger than expected full year sales, and upgraded their revenue forecast for next year, not something you would expect if the iPhone X was bombing as some seem to believe.
Of course, the good results at both of those suppliers could be down to other things, and as such misleading. It is also possible that this time the analysts have not erred on the side of caution, but that would mean there were a whole host of leopards out there with rearranged spots.
Overall, what looks far more likely is that once again AAPL is being sold due to a “...they can’t keep succeeding, can they?” feeling. I learned a long time ago that when faced with a choice between feelings and facts, facts win most of the time. In this case, the facts and history both point to this drop representing value, so at the very least investors should be holding onto AAPL and the more adventurous among you may consider buying going into earnings.
